collection.title: BIRTH SPACING AND UNDER-FIVE CHILD SURVIVAL IN GHANA: EVIDENCE FROM THE 2022 DEMOGRAPHIC AND HEALTH SURVEY.
collection.authors: Siddiq, A. I.; Akuffo, J. A.; Oppong, A. G.; Ditchfield, A.-M. X.; Agyarko Duah, S.; Lamptey, G. L.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Public Health, Faculty of Medical Sciences, Presbyterian University, Ghana.
collection.abstract:
BackgroundShort birth intervals are a well-documented, modifiable risk factor for child death in low- and middle-income countries, yet nationally representative evidence from Ghanas most recent Demographic and Health Survey has not been fully examined. This study assessed the association between the preceding birth interval and under-five mortality using the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey.

MethodsThe analysis used the complete birth history reported by women aged 15-49 years. The cohort comprised births occurring 60-119 completed months (5-10 years) before the survey, which allowed a complete five-year observation window for under-five survival (n = 8,418; 397 deaths). Spacing models were restricted to second-or-higher-order births with a defined preceding interval (n = 6,340; 282 deaths), categorised as under 18, 18-23, 24-35 (reference), 36-47, and 48 or more months. Crude and adjusted odds ratios were estimated using survey-weighted, Taylor-linearised logistic regression, adjusting for birth order, child sex, plurality, maternal age, residence, region, maternal education, wealth quintile, and marital status.

ResultsWeighted under-five mortality in the cohort was 45.4 per 1,000 live births (4.54%). Among second-or-higher-order births, weighted mortality fell from 9.3% after intervals of under 18 months and 8.0% after 18-23 months to 4.2%, 3.2%, and 3.5% after 24-35, 36-47, and 48 or more months, respectively. Relative to 24-35 months, the adjusted odds of death were higher after intervals of under 18 months (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 2.58, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.48-4.49, p < 0.001) and 18-23 months (AOR 2.09, 95% CI 1.33-3.29, p = 0.001); longer intervals did not differ from the reference. Multiple birth (AOR 2.48, 95% CI 1.33-4.63) and having a mother who was never in union (AOR 3.25, 95% CI 1.29-8.17) were also associated with higher odds of death, and marked regional variation persisted after adjustment.

ConclusionA short preceding birth interval, particularly one of under 18 months, was independently associated with an approximately two-to two-and-a-half-fold increase in the odds of under-five death in this nationally representative sample. The findings support continued investment in postpartum family planning to help women space births at least 24 months apart, alongside closer attention to multiple births, unmarried mothers, and the regions carrying the greatest burden.

collection.title: Diagnostic accuracy of deep learning for microsatellite instability prediction in gastric cancer: A systematic review and meta-analysis
collection.authors: Du, Y.; Liao, H.; Li, J.; He, Y.; Di, J.
collection.abstract: Deep learning (DL) applied to haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained pathology images can predict microsatellite instability (MSI) in gastric cancer (GC). We evaluated its diagnostic accuracy and discriminative performance. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library and Web of Science were searched for studies applying DL to H&E images for MSI prediction in GC. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261503140). Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated with a bivariate random-effects model, with subgroup analyses by validation strategy and data source; slide-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled after logit transformation. Prespecified scenario analyses assessed robustness. Ten studies were included; seven independent datasets from six studies entered the primary synthesis. Pooled sensitivity, specificity and summary receiver operating characteristic AUC were 0.78 (95% CI 0.63-0.88), 0.85 (95% CI 0.77-0.90) and 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.91); nine studies contributed to the secondary AUC synthesis (pooled AUC 0.85, 95% CI 0.80-0.89). Hospital-derived cohorts showed numerically higher sensitivity (0.86) and diagnostic odds ratio (39.8) than TCGA-derived cohorts (0.71 and 11.5), but subgroup differences were limited by the small number of studies and substantial heterogeneity. DL models show good diagnostic accuracy for MSI prediction in GC, but clinical utility still requires confirmation in standardised multicentre, independent external and prospective studies.

collection.title: The extent and durability of improvement in depressive symptoms, quality of life, and daily function with three years of vagus nerve stimulation in markedly treatment-resistant depression: A RECOVER study report
collection.authors: Conway, C. R.; Aaronson, S. T.; Rush, A. J.; Lee, Y.-C.; Gordon, C.; Shy, O.; Bunker, M. T.; Riva-Posse, P.; George, M. S.; Zajecka, J.; Nahas, Z.; Dunner, D. L.; de Quevedo, J. L.; Figee, M.; Mickey, B. J.; Allen, R. M.; Reeves, K.; Bohnenkamp, D.; Kriedt, C. L.; Hristidis, V. C.; Zorumski, C. F.; Macaluso, M.; Duffy, W.; Sheline, Y.; Alva, G.; Cusin, C.; Bennett, J. I.; Tran, Q.; McIntyre, R. S.; McAllister-Williams, R. H.; Sackeim, H. A.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, Washington University in St Louis, St Louis, MO, United States
collection.abstract:
BackgroundIn markedly treatment-resistant depression, the RECOVER trial compared the time course, extent, and durability of benefits in groups randomized to three years of active VNS (Early-Active) or one year of sham VNS followed by two years of active VNS (Delayed-Active).

MethodsFor 436 participants completing month-12 (M12) assessments (Early-Active N=221; Delayed-Active N=215), longitudinal mixed-effects models characterized trajectories of benefit over 36 months in categorical outcomes pooled across blinded depressive symptom and global improvement measures. Additional analyses examined the proportions benefiting and the degree and durability of benefits.

ResultsThe Early-Active group had greater odds of improvement during the RCT phase (OR=1.66; 95% CI=1.17-2.35; P=0.005). This between-group difference increased until M12 and then progressively narrowed upon VNS activation in the Delayed-Active group, approaching parity by M36. Across both groups, emergence of new beneficiaries plateaued after 24 months of active VNS, but with participants progressively achieving higher degrees of benefit thereafter. Following activation, the Delayed-Active group had significant improvement in all six categorical outcome measures. Durability was strong across depressive symptoms, function, and quality-of-life outcomes. For participants receiving active VNS throughout, durability of response was 70% from M12 to M36.

ConclusionsActive VNS was associated with improved benefits for both treatment groups over years 2 and 3. New beneficiaries emerged during the first two years of active VNS with continued progression to higher levels of benefit in the third year. These clinical benefits were highly durable. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03887715.

collection.title: Long-Term Impact of Stressful Life Events on Breast Cancer Risk: A 36-Year Genetically Informed Prospective Study in the Finnish Twin Cohort
collection.authors: Azzi, E.; Bode, H.; Palviainen, T.; Hukkanen, M.; Ollikainen, M.; Kaprio, J.
collection.abstract: Breast cancer (BC) is influenced by both genetic and environmental factors, but the long-term impact of stressful life events (SLEs) remains unclear. We examine the association between SLEs and BC risk using cohort and twin-pair analyses with 36 years of follow-up in the Finnish Twin Cohort, including 10,342 women and 719 BC cases. SLEs were assessed in 1981 by a questionnaire, while cancer incidence and mortality data were obtained from Finnish registries. Polygenic risk score for breast cancer (PRS-BC) and DNA methylation (DNAm) profiling were used to explore the underlying genetic and epigenetic factors. Cox proportional hazards models showed a significant association between SLEs and breast cancer risk (HR = 1.05 per event, 95% CI 1.02-1.08). As few as 2-3 SLEs were associated with a 24% increased risk (HR = 1.24, 95% CI 1.00-1.54), emphasizing the impact of even a modest number of events. Within-pair analyses in monozygotic twins suggested non-genetic factors mediate this association. Stratification by birth cohort revealed a stronger effect in women born before 1950 (HR = 1.07, 95% CI 1.01-1.12). While PRS-BC was not significantly associated with breast cancer risk, DNAm analysis identified 42 BC-associated CpG sites linked to both SLE exposure and environmental BC risk. These findings were replicated in cancer-free twin pairs, supporting epigenetic rather than genetic mediation. SLEs may be an independent risk factor for breast cancer, potentially mediated by epigenetic mechanisms. Further research is needed to explore the functional consequences of stress-related epigenetic changes and their role in BC development across generations.
